content: Bacteriostatic antibiotics function by inhibiting the growth and proliferation of bacteria. They achieve this by interfering with critical bacterial processes, including protein synthesis, DNA replication, and cellular metabolism. Unlike bactericidal agents, which directly kill bacteria, bacteriostatic agents do not destroy the microorganisms. Instead, they suppress bacterial growth, allowing the host's immune system to eliminate the pathogens from the body. It is important to note that the distinction between bacteriostatic and bactericidal agents is not always absolute. At higher concentrations, many bacteriostatic agents can exhibit bactericidal properties, while at lower concentrations, bactericidal agents may only act in a bacteriostatic manner. Examples of bacteriostatic agents include tetracyclines, sulphonamides, spectinomycin, trimethoprim, chloramphenicol, macrolides, and lincosamides.
